newsitem.title: USA: Orange County bankruptcy trial goes to jury.
newsitem.headline: Orange County bankruptcy trial goes to jury.

text.p: A prosecutor on Tuesday urged jurors to convict Orange County, California's former assistant treasurer Matthew Raabe of misappropriating public funds as the bankruptcy trial entered its final stage.
"The evidence is absolutely overwhelming that Mr. Raabe is guilty of each and every count," Assistant Orange County District Attorney Jan Nolan told jurors in Santa Ana.
Raabe's attorney, Gary Pohlson, countered in his closing remarks: "There has never been a more not-guilty person than Matthew Raabe."
Jurors were expected to begin deliberations on Wednesday.
Orange County filed for bankruptcy in December 1994 after sustaining losses of more than $1.6 billion on risky investments. The county emerged from bankruptcy last June.
In May 1995, Raabe was indicted by the county grand on several felony counts.

The District Attorney alleges that he helped to divert nearly $90 million in interest earnings owed to cities, schools and special districts that invested in the county investment pool before the county descended into bankruptcy.
"The evidence clearly proves to you that he appropriated the money of the pool participants to use in the county general fund," Nolan told jurors Tuesday.
Nolan said Raabe's strategy was:"You take it (money) from the rich and you give it to the poor. The only problem was, the pool participants weren't rich."
"We'll probably never know how many school books were never bought or teachers were never hired because they (pool investors) didn't get their money," Nolan said.
Raabe took notes on a yellow legal pad throughout the hearing and reacted by shaking his head during the prosecution's closing arguments.
Pohlson told jurors that Raabe believed the interest diversions were in fact legal.
"He believed it absolutely to be lawful and it probably is lawful," Raabe's attorney said.
"Matthew Raabe conducted himself as a good, honest person from day one with this county," he added.
Raabe was one of several Orange County officials to face charges following the bankruptcy.
In April 1995, former Orange County Treasurer Robert Citron pleaded guilty to six felonies for his role in the crisis.
A judge last November ordered him to spend a year in jail and pay a $100,000 fine, but Citron was later assigned to a community work program instead of jail.
Last October, a judge sentenced former Orange County budget director Ronald Rubino to probation for charges stemming from the investment crisis.
Citron has repeatedly claimed that Raabe was the "mastermind" behind the scheme to divert the interest earnings.

The prosecution said it is irrelevant who came up with the plan. "Mr. Raabe is guilty if it was Mr. Citron's idea, just as Mr. Citron was guilty if it was Mr. Raabe's idea," Nolan said during her closing arguments.
Pohlson argued that both men were not guilty. "Mr. Citron pled guilty to crimes he didn't commit," Raabe's attorney told the jury.
